description: Width tiers for Languages — F-10 sequence, Foundation band. All standards are capability descriptors. C strand standards use task_contexts as the primary width axis. U strand standards use phenomena_contexts (Systems of language) or phenomena_contexts (Language and culture). Foundation descriptors are thin — command terms are 'recognise', 'explore' — so minimum floors are intentionally narrow and wider tiers are modest.
subject: Languages

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single task context or phenomenon that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For C strand: minimum is the narrowest communicative context in which the described recognition or communication is genuine — not silent observation only. For U strand: minimum is noticing or exploring at least one instance of the described feature with evidence of awareness.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in elaboration cases. For C strand: a range of routine communicative contexts that reflect the descriptor's interactional intent. For U strand: the range of language features and cultural connections described in the elaborations.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new communicative contexts, cultural communities or language features. Width adds breadth of context — not difficulty of the same task. At Foundation, wider directions are appropriately modest — they extend the range of contexts engaged with, not the cognitive demand.
width_notes.elaborations: Target language (F-10 sequence) elaborations were used as the primary source. All target-language-specific vocabulary examples have been genericised. Elaborations are preserved verbatim in each standard entry as source record.

AC9LSF01.minimum_width: Respond appropriately (verbally or non-verbally) to at least three familiar target language words or routine instructions when supported by gesture, visual cues or context; use at least one modelled greeting or formulaic phrase.
AC9LSF01.typical_width: Participate in a range of classroom routines and communicative contexts — greetings and farewells, self-introduction elements, classroom instructions, likes and dislikes, familiar songs and games — using modelled words, gestures and formulaic phrases. Recognise and respond to meaning across varied routine contexts with support.
wider: Use target language expressions in a non-routine context — e.g. responding to a guest speaker, a new game, or a novel classroom situation — demonstrating transfer beyond rehearsed routines
Use target language to communicate a genuine personal reaction or preference in an unscripted moment, not only in response to a teacher prompt
Compare how a familiar communicative act (greeting, expressing a like) is done in the target language and in the student's home language — identify one similarity and one difference
elaborations: using common greetings and gestures appropriate to the time of day
using modelled language to introduce themselves with gestures such as pointing to self, holding up fingers
participating in class activities, routines and following instructions
listening to teacher's instructions and using non-verbal cues to label, match, circle, cross out, join, draw items
contributing to class activities and resources that involve naming, illustrating and matching
naming family members, friends and pets using props such as photos, pictures or toys
participating in group songs, chants and rhymes that have familiar tune or rhythm, with movement and dance
demonstrating likes and dislikes using simple statements with props
using target language versions of spontaneous exclamations or phrases to express dislike or likes
using formulaic expressions with others to offer congratulations, praise or to express well wishes related to special occasions
exploring simple numbers and counting through activities
imitating appropriate pronunciation and incorporating appropriate gestures, facial expressions and body language when interacting with others

AC9LSF02.minimum_width: Notice and imitate at least two sounds or letter patterns in the target language; identify at least one as similar to English and one as different.
AC9LSF02.typical_width: Explore a range of sound, letter and grammatical features of the target language — including sounds not present in English, basic noun features (e.g. gender markers), word order differences, and simple negation patterns — noticing similarities and differences with English. Participate in alphabet games, songs and activities that highlight sound-letter relationships.
wider: Notice and explain a specific phonetic or structural feature of the target language that differs from English — attempting to describe what is physically different about producing it
Identify target language-English cognates independently and explain what makes them recognisable across languages
Compare a simple target language sentence with its English equivalent — identify every word order or structural difference
elaborations: tracing letters and common words in the target language and English, identifying some similarities and differences
playing alphabet games and songs, imitating sounds, intonation patterns and tongue placement
noticing words that have similar pronunciation in the target language and English (cognates)
starting to notice the gender of nouns by listening to differences and using a range of props and visual cues
participating in target language versions of children's songs, games and rhymes, identifying some similarities and differences compared with English versions
observing simple noun+adjective word order differences
demonstrating early literacy skills by noticing phonetic similarities and differences between the target language and English
using simple negation patterns with formulaic language and gestures

AC9LSF03.minimum_width: Identify at least one target language word or expression that connects to a cultural practice — describe the connection in simple terms.
AC9LSF03.typical_width: Explore connections between the target language and the cultural practices of target language communities — including greetings and forms of address, celebrations, food, and formal/informal address conventions. Notice that the target language is spoken by many different communities. Engage with First Nations Australian language connections to Country and place.
wider: Compare a target language cultural practice (e.g. a celebration, a greeting convention) with a practice from the student's own background — identify what is similar and what is different
Find one local First Nations place name and connect it to the idea that language is tied to people and place — compare this with a target language community's relationship to place
Explore the languages spoken by class members and discuss what it means to speak more than one language — connecting to the target language community's multilingual contexts
elaborations: exploring the use of formal and informal ways of addressing people, and understanding that language can convey manners and respect
understanding that the target language is spoken in many places in the world
exploring different languages and cultures of class members and identifying different ways of greeting and expressing common terms
using the AIATSIS map of the languages of Australia to notice the language(s) of First Nations Australians in their local area
noticing how local names of streets, places and landmarks can have their origins in First Nations Australian languages
engaging with authentic visual resources to explore target language communities' celebrations, customs and food
looking at some familiar words for foods and their origins
understanding that there are many different languages in the world and that some people may speak more than one language
